svg.title: Reasoning Within the Text: assumptions and functions
svg.desc: Left panel, five kinds of unstated assumption with an example of each: causal, assuming A causes B when the evidence only shows they co-occur; representativeness, assuming one case or sample stands for the whole; definitional, assuming a contested term has a settled meaning; continuity, assuming what held before will keep holding; and value, assuming one priority outweighs another without defending it. Below them, the negation test: negate the candidate assumption, and if the argument collapses it is a real assumption, but if the argument survives it is not. Right panel, the function taxonomy, answering why an element is in the passage: support or illustration, concession or counterargument, qualification, contrast or juxtaposition, analogy or comparison, transition or signpost, and establishing stakes. Below it, the four traps: too strong, where the answer claims more than the argument requires; stated not assumed, where the answer paraphrases something the author actually wrote, which makes it a premise rather than an assumption; out of scope, where the answer is merely consistent with the argument rather than required by it; and distortion, where the answer describes what an element says instead of what it does. A footer notes that Reasoning Within the Text is about 30 percent of CARS questions, and that for a function question the right answer names the element's role, not its subject.
svg.text: Reasoning Within the Text: assumptions and functions
Two jobs: find the unstated premise holding the argument up, and say why an element is there.
Five kinds of unstated assumption
Causal
A causes B — but the evidence only shows they co-occur
Representativeness
one case or sample stands for the whole
Definitional
a contested term has a settled meaning
Continuity
what held before will keep holding
Value
this priority outweighs that one, undefended
The negation test
Negate the candidate assumption. If the argument collapses, it is
a real assumption. If the argument survives, it is not — and that
choice is out of scope.
Why is this element here?
Support / illustration — backs a claim
Concession / counterargument — grants or raises an objection
Qualification — narrows a claim to make it defensible
Contrast — sets two things side by side
Analogy — borrows force from a familiar case
Transition — moves the argument to its next phase
Establishing stakes — says why it matters
Four traps
· Too strong — claims more than the argument requires
· Stated, not assumed — it's a premise, not an assumption
· Out of scope — consistent with, but not required by
· Distortion — describes what it says, not what it does
Reasoning Within the Text is ~30% of CARS. For a function question, name the element's ROLE — not its subject.
